say.text: Two patients, one gallbladder, two different questions. Read each stem for its key word.
Case A: 34-year-old woman, RUQ pain for 2 days, fever, positive Murphy's sign, seen in clinic. Which test do you order first?

choices.label: HIDA scan of the gallbladder and ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Ultrasound is the initial investigation for gallstones and for suspected acute cholecystitis, and it detects gallstones with a sensitivity above 95%.
Hint: this stem asks what you order first from a clinic, not which test is most accurate. Think about the test every gallstone question starts with.
Not the right choice. HIDA is tempting because it is the most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis.
But this stem asks for the first test. HIDA is a confirmatory test, used when the first look is unclear.

sure_note.text: You were sure of HIDA. Its strength is accuracy, not order: it confirms cystic duct obstruction when the first test is equivocal.

say.text: Not the right choice. CT feels like the complete scan for abdominal pain with fever.
CT is kept for complications and for excluding other diagnoses, and it misses many gallstones, so it is not the first gallbladder test.

sure_note.text: You were sure of CT. It answers complications, not the first gallbladder question.

say.text: Two words, two tests. 'First' means the cheap test that opens the gallbladder question; 'most accurate' means the confirmatory test.
Ultrasound shows echogenic stones with shadowing, a thick wall and a sonographic Murphy's sign. HIDA settles it when ultrasound is unclear.
Case B: septic post-operative patient. Ultrasound is equivocal, and you need to know whether the cystic duct is blocked.
Which finding, on which test, confirms cystic duct obstruction?

choices.label: No gallbladder filling on HIDA with duodenal tracer
Wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid on CT
Dilated duct with a stone seen on MRCP
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The gallbladder does not fill while the tracer reaches the duodenum, which means the cystic duct is blocked.
Hint: this is the gallbladder's own function, not an image of the wall or the duct. What does a tracer show when the gallbladder fails to fill?
Not the right choice. Wall thickening and fluid are real signs of acute cholecystitis, so the finding feels like the answer.
But those are imaging signs of inflammation, and CT is for complications. The question asks which test shows the cystic duct is blocked.

sure_note.text: You were sure of CT. Wall signs support the diagnosis; they do not show whether the cystic duct is blocked.

say.text: Not the right choice. MRCP is tempting because the duct is the vessel you worry about, and it images it well.
A stone in the common duct is a different question from obstruction of the cystic duct. MRCP answers the duct question, not the gallbladder function.

sure_note.text: You were sure of MRCP. It finds common duct stones; it does not show whether the gallbladder is blocked.

say.text: Keep each test's job apart. Ultrasound opens the gallbladder question, HIDA confirms it, and MRCP answers the common bile duct.
Next, the duct. Here the order changes.
Case C: jaundiced patient, gallstones on ultrasound, and a common bile duct stone suspected. You want to confirm it without a procedure.
Which investigation do you order next?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is kept for when a stone must be treated.
Hint: the stem asks about the duct and says no procedure. Which test images the duct without going into it?
Not the right choice. ERCP is tempting because it both finds and removes duct stones, so it feels like the complete test.
It is therapeutic as well as diagnostic. This stem asks for the test you do without a procedure.

sure_note.text: You were sure of ERCP. It is the treatment step for a duct stone; the first test is the one that needs no procedure.

say.text: Not the right choice. Ultrasound is tempting because it found the gallstones in the first place.
It shows gallbladder stones well, but for duct stones the non-invasive test is MRCP. Repeating the same scan does not answer the duct question.

sure_note.text: You were sure of ultrasound. It answers the gallbladder question; the duct needs its own test.

say.text: Case D: Murphy's sign and fever on examination. Ultrasound now shows wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid.
What TG18 level is this patient at?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Suspected needs one local and one systemic sign. Imaging that shows the characteristic findings is the third set, and it makes the diagnosis definite.
Hint: TG18 has three sets. Two of them give the suspected level. What is the third set, and what happens when it is present?
Not the right choice. Suspected is tempting because Murphy's sign and fever are both present, and that pair is the suspected set.
But TG18 has a third set, imaging findings. Reread how the three sets fit together.

sure_note.text: You were sure it stayed suspected. Imaging is the third TG18 set, so once it shows the characteristic findings the level rises.

say.text: Not the right choice. This feels right because a rule that rests on two signs seems to need one more clinical sign.
The rule already has a local and a systemic sign. The missing piece is imaging, not another examination finding.

sure_note.text: You were sure a second local sign was needed. TG18 adds imaging as the third set, not another examination finding.

say.text: The ladder: ultrasound first, HIDA when the gallbladder question is unclear, MRCP for the duct, ERCP to treat, CT for complications.
TG18: one local plus one systemic sign gives suspected, and adding imaging gives definite.
